intro: Applied electrophysiology covers the recordings of the brain's electrical activity that psychiatrists use most: the electroencephalogram (EEG), its quantitative form (QEEG) and cerebral evoked potentials. This entry explains how the EEG is recorded and activated (Figure 33-33), the normal waking and sleep tracings and the four basic waveforms (Figure 33-34), the warning signs that suggest a hidden medical cause of a psychiatric presentation (Table 33-8), common EEG abnormalities (Table 33-9), the EEG effects of medications and drugs (Table 33-10) and the EEG changes seen in medical and psychiatric disorders (Tables 33-11 and 33-12). Update boxes add the current status of QEEG for diagnosis, what is now known about clozapine and the EEG, today's sleep-stage labels (N1 to N3 and R) and how to read the psychiatric EEG findings in Table 33-12.
objectives: Describe how an EEG is recorded, including the 10-20 electrode system and the main activation procedures.
Name the four basic waking waveforms with their frequency ranges and describe the normal sleep EEG.
Recognize the warning signs that suggest a medical or organic cause behind a psychiatric presentation.
Identify common EEG abnormalities and the EEG effects of psychotropic medications and drugs of abuse.
Summarize EEG changes in medical and psychiatric disorders.
Explain what QEEG and evoked potentials measure, and why they are not diagnostic tests for psychiatric disorders.
